This survey was done to check on the success of the walleye, muskellunge and largemouth bass introductions of 1967 and '68. Following the partial chemical treatment of August, 1967, the following introductions were made: (1) 1.5 million walleye fry planted 5/6/68, (2) 1500 Tiger muskellunge (x 7.2") planted 7/10/68, (3) and 2225 Fingerling LMB (x 2.3") planted 11/67. Only one floodlight on shocking craft was operating so collecting efficiency was down, but the sample obtained gives a good picture of the population structure in general. Approximately 12 additional muskys were turned over but not captured, plus innumerable walleyes. One 6.8" inch left pelvic clip LMB was taken, this being from the 1967 plant.

Three chemical and temperature stations were establish on Crystal Lake. Station 1 was in the outlet, Station 2 at the inlet, an Station 3 a vertical series in the deepest part of the lake. Since no thermocline had formed and the water was practically homogeneous chemically, no other stations were considered to be necessary. Perhaps if these conditions are checked later in the summer a more complicated situation may be found.

The transition area between sand and muck is quite extensive, as were shown on the map. This area was colored a mixture of yellow, representing sand, and brown, representing muck. At the East end of the lake the marl bottom type grades into muck and sand and this area is represented on the map by a mixture of yellow, brown and green. This mixed bottom (marl, muck and sand) type was found, only in T26N, R15W sections 22, 21 and 15. The bottom type considered marl was of a peculiar consistency not in common with true marl. A sample of this bottom preserved for verification was identified as marl.

REMARKS: Special reference should be made concerning the numerous fish found dead washed upon the shore, apparently killed by a fungus. Specimens were sent packed in ice to the Institute for Fisheries Research in hope that the causative organism could be ascertained. On a measured shore line 246 feet in length 66 dead bluegills were found. In another area 100 yards in length 100 dead fish were also found. In addition to bluegills, a few scattered specimens of sucker sp.?, bullheads, and perch were also found. In all cases the more mature fish were affected, fingerlings and fry were apparently "immune". . The entire lake had no steep shore. Roads extended to almost any point around it.
